questions.question_text: Which comparison of $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{8}$ is correct?

options.why: This treats the larger denominator as giving the larger unit fraction.
This treats equal numerators as making the fractions equal despite their different denominators.

questions.solution_text:
Thirds are larger pieces than eighths.
$\frac{1}{3}>\frac{1}{8}$

options.why: The largest denominator gives the smallest unit fraction.
An eighth is smaller than a fourth.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest denominator is $4$.
$\frac{1}{4}$ is greatest.

options.why: This selects the largest denominator, which gives the smallest unit fraction.
This overlooks that sixths are larger pieces than ninths.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest denominator is $6$.
$\frac{1}{6}$ is largest.

questions.question_text: In left-to-right number-line order, which comes first: $\frac{1}{6}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$?

options.why: A fourth is larger and therefore lies farther right.
Different unit fractions do not name the same point.

questions.question_text: Which order is correct for one tenth and one sixth?

options.why: This applies whole-number order without reversing for unit fractions.
Different positive denominators give different unit fractions.

questions.solution_text:
Tenths are smaller parts than sixths.
$\frac{1}{10}<\frac{1}{6}$

questions.question_text: A student writes $\frac{1}{143}>\frac{1}{87}$ because $143>87$. Which correction and explanation are correct?

options.text: $\frac{1}{143}<\frac{1}{87}$ because splitting the same whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller.
$\frac{1}{143}>\frac{1}{87}$ because the larger denominator gives the larger fraction.
options.why: This repeats the student's mistake of applying whole-number order to the denominators.
This ignores that the different denominators give pieces of different sizes.

questions.solution_text:
Splitting the same whole into $143$ equal pieces gives smaller pieces than splitting it into $87$ equal pieces.
$\frac{1}{143}<\frac{1}{87}$
